## Input data

The input files are the `*.filtered_variants.csv` files of six Tapestri libraries (listed in `load_data.py`), each containing one patient. They contain the variants that passed the Mosaic filters. The columns are:

- `CHR`, `POS`, `REF`, `ALT`, `REGION`, `NAME`, `FREQ`: variant information.
- One column per cell barcode, with entries `RO:AD:GT`: reference read count, alternative read count, and the Mosaic genotype call (0 = wildtype, 1 = heterozygous, 2 = homozygous, 3 = missing).

## Load data

For each library, `load_data()` (in `load_data.py`, shared by the notebooks in this directory) returns three tables with variants as rows and cells as columns: the read depth (`RO + AD`), the alternative read count (`AD`) and the genotype call. Each table has a `variant` column (`CHR:POS:REF/ALT`) followed by one column per cell barcode. All three are built from the same input rows and columns, so rows and columns are in the same order and can be combined element-wise without worrying about mismatches.

```{python}
#| label: load-data
#| echo: true

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import polars as pl
from scipy import stats

from load_data import load_data

data = load_data()
libraries = list(data)

for b, (depth, alt, gt) in data.items():
    assert depth.columns == alt.columns == gt.columns
    assert depth['variant'].equals(alt['variant']) and depth['variant'].equals(gt['variant'])
    print(f'{b}: {depth.height} variants x {depth.width - 1} cells')
```


## Homozygous sites

At a homozygous site, every read of the other allele is an error: reference reads at homozygous mutated (alt/alt) sites, and alt reads at homozygous wildtype (ref/ref) sites. We expect the two cases to behave symmetrically, and model the error read count of a cell as

$$
\text{errors} \sim \text{Binom}(\text{depth}, p),
$$

with error rate $p$. We check (1) whether the binomial is adequate or the data are overdispersed, (2) whether $p$ depends on the locus, and (3) whether mutated and wildtype sites indeed behave alike.

A locus counts as homozygous mutated (wildtype) in a library if at least 80% of its called cells (genotype ≠ 3) are called homozygous mutated (wildtype). We use all cells with depth ≥ 1 at these loci.

Note that the input contains only variants that passed the Mosaic filters, which require a variant to be mutated in at least 1% of the cells. A mostly wildtype locus therefore only enters the data if it shows alt reads in some cells; clean wildtype loci were filtered out. The wildtype loci here are thus a selected, noisier subset.

```{python}
#| label: hom-data
#| echo: true

from scipy import optimize, special

SITE_TYPES = {'hom mutated': 2, 'hom wildtype': 0}  # genotype call of the type

hom = {}
for b, (depth, alt, gt) in data.items():
    depth_b, alt_b, gt_b = (t.drop('variant').to_numpy() for t in (depth, alt, gt))
    called = gt_b != 3
    for site_type, genotype in SITE_TYPES.items():
        loci = ((gt_b == genotype) & called).sum(axis=1) / called.sum(axis=1) >= 0.8
        locus, cell = np.nonzero(loci[:, None] & (depth_b >= 1))
        errors = depth_b - alt_b if site_type == 'hom mutated' else alt_b
        hom[b, site_type] = {
            'errors': errors[locus, cell],
            'depth': depth_b[locus, cell],
            'locus': np.unique(locus, return_inverse=True)[1],  # 0, ..., n_loci - 1
            'n_loci': int(loci.sum()),
        }
        print(f"{b}, {site_type}: {hom[b, site_type]['n_loci']} loci, {len(locus)} observations")
```

### Binomial fit and overdispersion

The maximum-likelihood estimate of $p$ is the total number of error reads divided by the total depth. To check for overdispersion we use

- the **Pearson dispersion** $\frac{1}{N - 1} \sum_i \frac{(\text{errors}_i - \text{depth}_i\, p)^2}{\text{depth}_i\, p (1 - p)}$, which is about 1 under the binomial and larger under overdispersion, and
- a **likelihood-ratio test** against a beta-binomial with the same mean $p$ and concentration $\kappa$ (smaller $\kappa$ means more overdispersion). As the binomial is the boundary case $\kappa \to \infty$, the LR statistic follows a 50:50 mixture of $\chi^2_0$ and $\chi^2_1$, i.e. p-value = $\frac{1}{2} P(\chi^2_1 > \text{LR})$.

We do this once with one $p$ for all loci of a library and site type (*shared*), and once with one $p$ per locus (*within locus*), to separate overdispersion between loci from overdispersion within a locus.

```{python}
#| label: hom-binomial
#| echo: true


def pearson_dispersion(k, n, p, n_params):
    """Pearson chi-square divided by its degrees of freedom; about 1 for binomial data."""
    return ((k - n * p) ** 2 / (n * p * (1 - p))).sum() / (len(k) - n_params)


def betabinom_neg_loglik(k, n, p_start):
    """Minimised negative log-likelihood and (p, kappa) of a beta-binomial fit."""

    def neg_loglik(theta):
        p, kappa = special.expit(theta[0]), np.exp(theta[1])
        return -stats.betabinom.logpmf(k, n, p * kappa, (1 - p) * kappa).sum()

    res = optimize.minimize(neg_loglik, [special.logit(p_start), np.log(100)], method='L-BFGS-B')
    return res.fun, special.expit(res.x[0]), np.exp(res.x[1])


rows = []
for (b, site_type), h in hom.items():
    k, n, locus, n_loci = h['errors'], h['depth'], h['locus'], h['n_loci']

    # Shared p for all loci of the library and site type.
    p = k.sum() / n.sum()
    nll_binom = -stats.binom.logpmf(k, n, p).sum()
    nll_bb, _, kappa = betabinom_neg_loglik(k, n, p)
    lr_od = 2 * (nll_binom - nll_bb)

    # One p per locus.
    p_locus = np.bincount(locus, weights=k) / np.bincount(locus, weights=n)
    p_locus = np.clip(p_locus, 1e-6, None)  # a locus without any error read would give p = 0
    nll_binom_locus = -stats.binom.logpmf(k, n, p_locus[locus]).sum()
    nll_bb_locus = sum(
        betabinom_neg_loglik(k[locus == l], n[locus == l], p_locus[l])[0] for l in range(n_loci)
    )
    lr_od_locus = 2 * (nll_binom_locus - nll_bb_locus)
    h['p'], h['p_locus'], h['nll_binom'], h['nll_binom_locus'] = p, p_locus, nll_binom, nll_binom_locus

    rows.append(
        {
            'library': b,
            'site type': site_type,
            'p (shared)': p,
            'Pearson dispersion (shared)': pearson_dispersion(k, n, p, 1),
            'kappa (shared)': kappa,
            'LR overdispersion (shared)': lr_od,
            'p-value (shared)': stats.chi2.sf(lr_od, 1) / 2,
            'Pearson dispersion (within locus)': pearson_dispersion(k, n, p_locus[locus], n_loci),
            'LR overdispersion (within locus)': lr_od_locus,
            'p-value (within locus)': stats.chi2.sf(lr_od_locus, n_loci) / 2,
        }
    )

pl.DataFrame(rows).sort('site type', 'library').with_columns(pl.col(pl.Float64).round(4))
```

The p-value for the within-locus test uses $\chi^2_L$ (one boundary parameter per locus, halved) as an approximation.

### Does the error rate depend on the locus?

Likelihood-ratio test of one $p$ per locus against one shared $p$ ($L - 1$ degrees of freedom), and the per-locus estimates.

```{python}
#| label: hom-locus
#| echo: true

rows = []
for (b, site_type), h in hom.items():
    lr = 2 * (h['nll_binom'] - h['nll_binom_locus'])
    df = h['n_loci'] - 1
    rows.append(
        {
            'library': b,
            'site type': site_type,
            'n_loci': h['n_loci'],
            'min p_locus': h['p_locus'].min(),
            'max p_locus': h['p_locus'].max(),
            'LR statistic': lr,
            'df': df,
            'p-value': stats.chi2.sf(lr, df),
        }
    )
display(pl.DataFrame(rows).sort('site type', 'library').with_columns(pl.col(pl.Float64).round(4)))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(libraries), figsize=(3 * len(libraries), 2.5), squeeze=False)
for ax, b in zip(axes[0], libraries):
    for site_type in SITE_TYPES:
        h = hom[b, site_type]
        line = ax.plot(np.sort(h['p_locus']), 'o', label=site_type)
        ax.axhline(h['p'], color=line[0].get_color(), ls='--')
    ax.set_yscale('log')
    ax.set_title(b, fontsize=8)
    ax.set_xlabel('locus (sorted)')
    ax.set_ylabel('error rate p')
axes[0, 0].legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8)
fig.suptitle('Per-locus error rates; dashed: shared estimate')
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### Distribution of the error rate across loci

As the error rate depends on the locus, we model it as a draw per locus,

$$
\text{logit}(p_l) \sim \text{Normal}(\mu, \tau),
$$

on the logit scale, as the per-locus rates span orders of magnitude and are bounded by 0. Each locus has tens to hundreds of thousands of reads, so the per-locus estimates are very precise compared with the spread between loci, and we estimate $\mu$ and $\tau$ directly from the per-locus estimates (with a continuity correction, $(k + 0.5) / (n + 1)$, for loci with very few error reads). We estimate them per site type, and test whether the two types differ (Welch's t-test on the logit error rates).

```{python}
#| label: hom-locus-distribution
#| echo: true

logit_p = {}
for (b, site_type), h in hom.items():
    k_l = np.bincount(h['locus'], weights=h['errors'])
    n_l = np.bincount(h['locus'], weights=h['depth'])
    logit_p[b, site_type] = special.logit((k_l + 0.5) / (n_l + 1))

pooled = {t: np.concatenate([z for (_, st), z in logit_p.items() if st == t]) for t in SITE_TYPES}
rows = [
    {'library': b, 'site type': t, 'n_loci': len(z), 'mu': z.mean(), 'tau': z.std(ddof=1)}
    for (b, t), z in logit_p.items()
] + [
    {'library': 'all', 'site type': t, 'n_loci': len(z), 'mu': z.mean(), 'tau': z.std(ddof=1)}
    for t, z in pooled.items()
]
display(
    pl.DataFrame(rows)
    .sort('site type', 'library')
    .with_columns(pl.col('mu').map_elements(special.expit, return_dtype=pl.Float64).alias('p at mu'))
    .with_columns(pl.col(pl.Float64).round(4))
)
print('Welch t-test, logit p of mutated vs. wildtype loci:', stats.ttest_ind(*pooled.values(), equal_var=False))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3))
for site_type, z in pooled.items():
    axes[0].hist(z, bins=20, alpha=0.5, label=site_type)
axes[0].set_xlabel('logit(p) per locus')
axes[0].legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8)
for ax, (site_type, z) in zip(axes[1:], pooled.items()):
    stats.probplot(z, dist='norm', plot=ax)
    ax.set_title(f'Q-Q plot, {site_type}')
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Are the error reads at wildtype loci only background noise? Per locus, the fraction of cells (depth ≥ 10) with an error-read fraction above 0.3, i.e. cells that look heterozygous rather than erroneous:

```{python}
#| label: hom-wildtype-outlier-cells
#| echo: true

for site_type in SITE_TYPES:
    fractions = []
    for b in libraries:
        h = hom[b, site_type]
        keep = h['depth'] >= 10
        high = (h['errors'][keep] / h['depth'][keep]) > 0.3
        fractions.append(np.bincount(h['locus'][keep], weights=high) / np.bincount(h['locus'][keep]))
    print(f'{site_type}: quantiles (10%, 50%, 90%) over loci:', np.quantile(np.concatenate(fractions), [0.1, 0.5, 0.9]).round(3))
```

At the wildtype loci, the error reads are not only background noise: a few percent of the cells (in some loci up to about 30%) look heterozygous, as expected for loci that passed the Mosaic filter because enough cells were called mutated. Together with the filter-driven selection, this explains why wildtype loci show far higher and less variable error rates than mutated loci, so the two cases do not behave symmetrically in this data.
